title: What If You Drank a Cup of Bacteria to Prove a Point? It Won a Nobel

scenes.text: What if you drank bacteria just to win an argument? In 1984, one doctor did.
Back then, stomach ulcers were blamed on stress. Patients got antacids and tranquilizers, sometimes surgery.
Two Australians, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, kept finding a spiral-shaped bacterium in inflamed stomachs. Almost nobody believed them.
They had no animal to test it on. So Marshall stirred the bacteria into a broth and swallowed it.
Within days came nausea, vomiting and foul breath. After ten days, a camera down his throat showed an inflamed stomach.
Antibiotics cleared it. In 2005 the two men shared a Nobel Prize, and ulcers turned out to be an infection you can treat.

description:
What if you drank a culture of bacteria to prove your theory?
In the early 1980s most doctors blamed stomach ulcers on stress and excess acid and treated them with antacids, tranquillisers and sometimes surgery. In Perth, pathologist Robin Warren and trainee doctor Barry Marshall kept finding a spiral bacterium, now called Helicobacter pylori, in inflamed stomach tissue, but the idea that a germ caused ulcers was dismissed. With no suitable animal to test it on, Marshall drank a broth containing the bacteria in 1984. Within days he developed nausea, vomiting and bad breath, and an endoscopy about ten days later showed his stomach lining was inflamed; a biopsy found the bacteria. He then took antibiotics. Marshall and Warren received the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Roughly half of all people carry the bacterium, and it is blamed for most stomach ulcers. This is history, not medical advice.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: He did it without asking an ethics board, or his wife. Which scientist's self-experiment should we run through next?
